blocks.text: Quick verdict

FloppyData is much cheaper for US and Western European traffic: $10 for 10 GB against $50 on SOAX's Sandbox, and $100 for 100 GB against about $300 on Builder, with no country tiers. SOAX is the better choice for ad verification, mobile-first testing and multi-country work that needs ISP or carrier targeting, a large published network (155M residential, 33M mobile) and UDP or QUIC. For high-stakes or precise work, SOAX's depth is worth paying for.

FloppyData and SOAX both put residential and mobile traffic on a single balance, which makes them interesting to compare. FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for everything, regardless of country or volume. SOAX charges credits whose per-GB rate depends on your plan and the exit country's tier, with credits expiring after 60 days, but offers a much larger network, ISP and carrier targeting and UDP and QUIC support. This comparison shows when each model wins.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData is a young budget provider registered in Dubai that launched around 2024. Its pitch is radical simplicity: one balance at a flat $1/GB that you can spend on residential, mobile or datacenter rotating traffic, plus static residential and datacenter IPs sold in monthly bundles. Its residential page lists home ISP IPs in 148 countries and 442 cities. The company also offers a free cloud anti-detect browser that runs on its proxies. Its advertised 65M+ IP figure has been questioned by some reviewers, and user reviews are mixed.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Pricing: FloppyData vs SOAX

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $10 with FloppyData and $50 with SOAX: a 80% saving in FloppyData's favour. For a 100 GB month, FloppyData costs about $100 while SOAX costs about $300, so FloppyData saves around 67%. Both FloppyData and SOAX work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and SOAX lists '155M residential + 33M mobile'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and SOAX lists 195. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. How FloppyData compares: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: city and ISP targeting for local results. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. How FloppyData compares: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: granular location filters. How FloppyData compares: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. The limitation on the FloppyData side: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the SOAX side: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and SOAX before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and SOAX is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 1, SOAX in 5, and 0 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
